body.heading: A very small worker with a very big job
paragraphs: Look at a bee and you might just see a small, stripy insect. Farmers see something else: one of the hardest-working partners they have. Bees are responsible, directly or indirectly, for about one out of every three bites of food you eat. Without them, supermarket shelves would look shockingly empty.
How does an insect the size of your thumb carry that much importance? It all starts with a flower's problem.

body.heading: Stop and think
paragraphs: Before you read on: a flower cannot walk. It stays rooted in one spot its whole life. But to make seeds — and fruit — most flowers need pollen from another flower. How do you think the pollen travels? Make a guess, then read on.

body.heading: Pollen's taxi service
paragraphs: Pollen is a flower's yellow dust, and it must reach another flower of the same kind for seeds and fruit to form. Wind carries some pollen, but bees are the master couriers. A bee visits a flower to drink its sweet nectar, and pollen sticks to her fuzzy body. At the next flower, some pollen rubs off. Flower fed, bee fed, seeds started.

This is called pollination, and bees do it billions of times a day — apples, berries, almonds, cucumbers, pumpkins and hundreds more foods all depend on it. A single honeybee colony can visit millions of flowers in a season, and one bee will visit fifty to a hundred flowers on a single trip.

body.heading: Words to know
paragraphs: Pollen — the yellow dust a flower makes, which must reach another flower for seeds to form.
Pollination — the carrying of pollen from flower to flower, often by bees.
Nectar — the sweet liquid flowers offer, which bees drink and turn into honey.
Colony — the whole bee family living together in one hive, led by a single queen.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Bees are in trouble in many places because of lost wildflowers, some farm sprays and disease. Which of the helping ideas in this article could your family actually do — plant a flower pot, leave a wild corner, buy local honey?

2. A bee stings only to defend itself or its hive, and a honeybee dies after stinging — so it is truly a last resort. How does knowing that change how you act near bees? (Calm and slow wins: never swat, just step away.)

takeaway: Bees carry pollen from flower to flower, making seeds and fruit possible — about one in three bites of our food starts with a bee's visit.
